summary: Bobby Tiernay and Kam Sween, engineers at Auth0/Okta, present on securing AI agents with open identity standards. They frame the problem around OWASP's "excessive agency" risk: agents calling APIs, pulling data, and using credentials without proper scoping, monitoring, or user attribution. A common anti-pattern uses shared static keys from environment variables—fragile, overly broad, and lacking audit trails. The preferred pattern has agents request tokens from a backend that performs token exchange to mint short-lived, user-specific, API-specific tokens that never sit with the agent. Identity is foundational: without it, agents run as service accounts, creating confused deputy problems. Standard flows—OAuth 2.1, RAR, and token exchange—anchor agent behavior to real users. For RAG, fine-grained authorization should be enforced at the retrieval layer, not delegated to the LLM. CIBA enables async human-in-the-loop approvals via push notifications to trusted devices, critical for headless or background agents. MCP servers moving from local to remote deployments need OAuth 2.1 flows with proper token binding. Kam then demonstrates a TypeScript CLI trading assistant bootstrapping an OIDC client via device flow for user authentication. A CIBA higher-order component intercepts sensitive tool calls, pausing execution to await user approval dispatched as a push notification containing specific action details—e.g., purchasing 10 shares on behalf of the user. A token vault manages tokens (not credentials) to avoid embedding client secrets in code. Once authenticated, subsequent trades no longer require UI interaction beyond the CIBA approval flow. Wi-Fi issues prevented the live demo from completing, but Kam walked through the expected flow. Bobby wraps up by noting that standards prevent reinvention, and Auth0 wraps these building blocks—including async CIBA confirmation, token exchange, token vault, and fine-grained RAG authorization—into a developer-friendly experience. OpenFGA is available as an open-source fine-grained authorization option. Bobby also participates in open MCP spec discussions and mentions MCP-O as another relevant open-source library. CIBA is GA or early access in the Auth0 platform.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Security Challenges of Smarter Agents
sections.summary: Bobby and Kam introduce themselves as Auth0/Okta engineers working on identity for agent-centric systems. They outline OWASP excessive agency risks: secrets in prompts, overly broad scopes, poor visibility, and sensitive data exposure. Agents now call APIs, kick off workflows, and touch real user data, requiring proper user-context authorization.

sections.title: Shared Keys vs. Token Exchange & Identity Foundations
sections.summary: Contrasts the common pattern of shared static keys from environment variables with token exchange for short-lived, user-specific, API-scoped tokens. Identity is foundational: without it, agents run as service accounts creating confused deputy problems. Standard flows—OAuth 2.1, RAR, token exchange—anchor behavior to real users. Tokens never sit with the agent; the backend fetches credentials from a vault and mints tokens on demand.

sections.title: RAG Authorization, CIBA & MCP Security
sections.summary: For RAG, fine-grained authorization must be enforced at the retrieval layer, not inside the LLM. CIBA enables async human-in-the-loop approvals via push notifications to trusted devices for headless agents. MCP servers moving to network deployments need OAuth 2.1 flows with proper token binding, as shared servers demand guarantees about who makes each request.

sections.title: Demo: CIBA Flow with TypeScript Trading Assistant
sections.summary: Kam demonstrates a TypeScript CLI AI trading assistant using three components: user identification and context, a token vault to avoid embedding secrets, and CIBA for user consent before executing trades. Shows agent configuration with generate_messages and main methods, tool call definitions wrapped in higher-order component functions, and context binding to threads for durable user identification.

sections.title: Demo Walkthrough & Token Vault Details
sections.summary: Kam details the use_device_flow handler for bootstrapping the OIDC client and the use_ciba higher-order component that intercepts tool calls requiring user approval with a blocking callback. The token vault on line 28 of the buy tool call manages tokens, not credentials, preventing embedded client secrets. Local AI agents still need identity, especially with multiple users or user data access. User authentication happens through the UI; subsequent sensitive actions use CIBA with no additional UI required.

sections.title: Live Demo Attempt & CIBA Notification Flow
sections.summary: Kam attempts to buy 10 stocks of SECO but Wi-Fi issues prevent live execution. He walks through the expected flow: middleware prompts login, agent receives tokens to act on the user's behalf, CIBA dispatches a notification to Auth0's backend and the user's phone with specific action details (purchasing 10 shares on your behalf), and the user can approve or cancel. After initial authentication, subsequent trades only require CIBA approval, not re-authentication.

sections.title: Wrap-Up: Standards, OpenFGA & MCP Spec
sections.summary: Kam summarizes three patterns: user identification acting on behalf of a specific user, secure credential storage via token vault, and CIBA for explicit approval of high-risk actions without a browser. Bobby notes Auth0 wraps these standards into a developer-friendly experience including async CIBA, token exchange, token vault, and fine-grained RAG authorization. OpenFGA is available as an open-source fine-grained authorization option. Bobby participates in open MCP spec discussions and highlights MCP-O as another open-source library. CIBA is GA or early access in Auth0's platform.
